claims.text: The initial titanium–nickel-containing high-entropy alloy is an as-cast, single-phase solid solution.
Controlled high-temperature aging will induce fine-scale secondary precipitates in the alloy.
The secondary precipitates will be dispersed within the primary matrix phase.
The secondary precipitates will obstruct dislocation motion at elevated temperatures.
Obstruction of dislocation motion by the precipitates will increase elevated-temperature yield strength.
Precipitation strengthening may enhance creep resistance under extreme-environment conditions.
The aged alloy will have greater elevated-temperature mechanical strength than the as-cast, single-phase control.
The magnitude of improvement will depend on the heat-treatment parameters.
Performance depends on aging temperature, aging duration, and resulting precipitate volume fraction.
The hypothesis is intended to apply only to the unspecified titanium–nickel high-entropy-alloy composition and to controlled elevated-temperature or extreme-environment test regimes.

contradictions.description: The conditions state that phase boundaries will be maintained, whereas the proposed intervention is explicitly intended to form secondary precipitate phases. If 'phase boundaries' means maintaining the original single-phase constitution, these requirements conflict.
